policy: Review every closed candidate set. Select only when ASV wording or an explicit mapped textual note distinguishes a reading; otherwise mark underdetermined and retain the base fallback. The base candidate is the qere, which is what MACULA Hebrew projects; the alternative is the ketiv written in the Leningrad Codex.

decisions.evidence: The readings differ in the object suffix: qere לַהֲשִׁיבָהּ 'to bring her back' against ketiv להשיבו 'to bring him back'. ASV renders 'to bring her again', a feminine object referring to the concubine, which matches the qere; the ketiv's masculine suffix would have given 'to bring him back'.

The readings differ only in the preposition on the infinitive: qere כַּעֲלוֹת (כְּ, 'as/when it came up') against ketiv בעלות (בְּ, 'at/when it came up'). Both yield the same temporal clause in English, and ASV's 'and when the day began to spring' does not distinguish כְּ from בְּ. No ASV note is mapped to this unit, so the base qere fallback carries the projection.
